title: Carbohydrate Structure and Function
scopeNote: Original condensed MCAT biochemistry lessons covering the declared outline sections. This release is implemented, not independently scientifically verified; it is not exhaustive textbook coverage.

steps.text: Monosaccharides can be classified by carbon number and carbonyl position. An aldose has an aldehyde in its open-chain form; a ketose has a ketone.
The D/L designation compares configuration at a reference stereocenter with glyceraldehyde. It does not specify the sign of optical rotation.
Enantiomers differ at every stereocenter. Epimers are diastereomers differing at one stereocenter; anomers differ at the anomeric carbon after cyclization.
Carbonyl classification and configuration are independent descriptors. A D sugar can be an aldose or a ketose, and ring formation does not erase its stereochemical identity.

steps.text: An intramolecular reaction between a hydroxyl and a carbonyl can form a cyclic hemiacetal or hemiketal. The original carbonyl carbon becomes the anomeric carbon.
Cyclization can create alpha and beta anomers. For common D sugars in a conventional Haworth drawing, alpha places the anomeric substituent opposite the reference CH2OH group.

steps.text: Glycosidic linkages specify the connected carbons and anomeric configuration. Glycogen has alpha(1→4) chains and alpha(1→6) branch points.
Cellulose contains beta(1→4)-linked glucose units. Human digestive enzymes do not efficiently hydrolyze these linkages, despite glucose being usable as a monomer.
Sucrose links both constituent anomeric carbons and is nonreducing. Lactose retains a free anomeric carbon and is reducing.
A branched glycogen particle has many nonreducing ends for synthesis and degradation. Branching does not create a free reducing end at every branch.
